title: Supporting future heart screening in newborn babies through testing of two oxygen sensors linked to a mobile app
official: Improving newborn screening for congenital heart disease using dual pulse oximeter signals and a mobile app: a feasibility study
summary:
Background and study aims
Congenital heart disease (CHD) affects around 6,000 newborn babies in the UK each year. Current national screening includes an ultrasound scan during pregnancy and a newborn examination after birth. Some hospitals also use pulse oximetry as an additional check, but some babies with CHD can still be missed.

Pulse oximeters are small sensors that measure blood oxygen levels and pulse rate. They also produce a pulse-wave signal containing information about the circulation. Comparing signals recorded at the same time from a baby’s upper and lower limbs may provide useful additional information. Pulse oximetry may also perform differently across different skin tones.
This study aims to find out whether two pulse oximeters connected to a mobile app can reliably collect good-quality signals from a newborn baby’s upper and lower limbs during newborn care. This study will also assess whether the approach is practical and acceptable to parents and NHS staff. The study is not designed to diagnose heart disease or determine whether this approach improves screening.

Who can participate?
Healthy babies born at term, term babies with suspected or confirmed congenital heart disease, and preterm babies with a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) who are receiving drug treatment as part of their usual clinical care. Parents or other people with parental responsibility may complete a questionnaire, and also be invited for an interview. NHS staff who have used the study system may complete a questionnaire, and be invited for an interview.

What does the study involve?
Two soft pulse-oximeter sensors are placed on the baby, one on the right hand or wrist and one on either foot. Once stable signals are obtained, oxygen saturation, pulse rate, pulse amplitude and pulse-wave signals from both limbs are recorded simultaneously for a target of five minutes using the research mobile app. Skin tone beside each sensor site is also assessed independently by two trained members of the study team using a six-tone shade card, and relevant information is collected from the medical record. The app is used only to collect research data and does not provide a screening result, diagnosis or treatment recommendation.

Healthy term babies usually have one recording. Babies with suspected or confirmed CHD may have a second recording after 24 hours of age or at routine follow-up at around one month. Preterm babies with PDA have recordings before and after clinically indicated drug treatment. Parents and staff may also be invited to complete short questionnaires and, for a smaller group, an optional interview about their experience of the study.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
There is no expected direct medical benefit to babies or other participants. The information gained may help researchers decide whether this approach should be investigated in a larger future study aimed at improving the early detection of congenital heart disease.

The study procedures are low risk and non-invasive. The sensors are routinely used in newborn care, although their placement may occasionally cause brief discomfort, temporary skin marking or disturbance. Clinical care will always take priority and a recording can be delayed or stopped if the baby becomes unsettled or unwell. Questionnaires and interviews require some additional time, and some parents may find discussing their experiences or their baby’s condition upsetting.

Where is the study run from?
The study is sponsored by University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust. Initial recruitment and data collection will take place at the Royal Sussex County Hospital, Brighton. Additional University Hospitals Sussex locations may be added later if required and appropriately approved.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
The first participant is expected to be enrolled in December 2026, with recruitment and participant data collection planned until April 2028. The overall research project funding runs until June 2028, allowing time for final analysis and reporting.

Who is funding the study?
The National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Research for Patient Benefit (RfPB) Programme, UK.

Who is the main contact?
Dr Ramon Fernandez, Chief Investigator, Brighton and Sussex Medical School, ramon.fernandez@nhs.net

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Newborn participants: Newborn babies receiving care through participating UHSx maternity, postnatal, neonatal, paediatric cardiology or follow-up pathways may be eligible if they fall into one of the following groups:
1.1. WP1: Healthy term newborns born at > = 37+0 weeks’ gestation who are clinically stable and undergoing or available for the routine newborn check, with recording planned during or around the newborn check, typically 4–8 hours after birth where clinically and practically appropriate.
1.2. WP2: Term newborns born at > = 37+0 weeks’ gestation with suspected or confirmed congenital heart disease, who are clinically stable enough to undergo a brief non-invasive recording and can attend or be accessed at the relevant follow-up site where applicable.
1.3. WP3: Preterm newborns born at < 37+0 weeks’ gestation with a patent ductus arteriosus confirmed on routine clinical echocardiography, where the clinical team has independently decided to undertake clinically indicated pharmacological treatment and considers the baby clinically stable enough for brief non-invasive probe placement and recording.
1.4. For all newborn participants, the responsible clinical team must consider dual-sensor pulse oximetry probe placement on the right hand or wrist and either foot clinically appropriate and safe. Written informed consent must be received from a parent or other person aged 16 years or over with parental responsibility before any research-specific procedure or extraction of clinical information for research.
1.5. Each newborn from a multiple pregnancy will be assessed independently against the relevant eligibility criteria, and consent will be received separately for each baby enrolled.

2. Parent/family questionnaire and interview participants:
2.1. One parent or other person with parental responsibility linked to each enrolled newborn may participate in the parent-facing study components. They must be aged 16 years or over, able and willing to provide informed consent for their own participation, and able to complete a questionnaire and/or take part in an interview in English or with approved language support where this is available and sufficient to support valid informed consent and meaningful participation.

3. Staff questionnaire and interview participants:
3.1. NHS staff, including midwives, neonatal nurses or doctors, who have used the dual-sensor app during the study and are willing to complete a questionnaire and/or take part in an interview.
Exclusion criteria:
1. Newborn participants: Newborn babies will not be enrolled where any of the following apply:
1.1. The newborn is acutely unwell, requires urgent clinical intervention, or is judged by the attending clinician to be clinically unstable such that the research procedure would be inappropriate or could interfere with clinical care
1.2. A skin condition, wound, dressing, bandage, splint, intravenous or arterial line, limb malformation, amputation, congenital abnormality, phototherapy equipment or other clinical equipment prevents simultaneous safe placement of one pulse oximetry sensor on the right hand or wrist and another on at least one foot
1.3. The same newborn has already been enrolled in another newborn work package or has been enrolled previously in the same work package. Planned repeat or paired recordings undertaken within the assigned work package are not considered duplicate enrolment.
1.4. An active safeguarding concern makes research approach inappropriate at that time
1.5. The attending clinician considers research approach or enrolment inappropriate for clinical, welfare or other reasons
1.6. Valid written informed consent has not been received from a parent or other person aged 16 years or over with parental responsibility
1.7. Parent or other person with parental responsibility who requires language support to provide valid informed consent, where sufficient approved language support, such as a professional interpreter and/or approved translated materials, cannot be arranged within the relevant clinical timeframe. Family members or untrained staff will not be used as interpreters for informed consent.
1.8. A parent aged under 16 years will not be asked to provide consent for the newborn's participation
1.9. Where another person aged 16 years or over with parental responsibility is available and able to provide informed consent, the newborn may still be considered for enrolment; otherwise, the newborn will not be enrolled

2. Parent/family questionnaire and interview participants: Parent/family participants will not be enrolled if they:
2.1. Are aged under 16 years
2.2. Are unable or unwilling to provide informed consent for their own participation
2.3. Lack capacity to provide informed consent
2.4. Cannot participate meaningfully in English and sufficient approved language support is unavailable

3. Staff questionnaire and interview participants: Staff will not be enrolled if they:
3.1. Have not used the dual-sensor app during the study
3.2. Are unable or unwilling to provide informed consent
3.3. Lack capacity to provide informed consent
